standard-description.text: What is the standard description of a machine?

steps.text: A list of the steps that the machine makes
steps.why: The steps depend on the input. The standard description holds only the rules.

rules-as-letters.text: Its rules, written as one line of letters
rules-as-letters.why: Each rule becomes five parts in letters, and a semicolon ends it.

tape.text: The symbols on its tape at the end
tape.why: The tape holds what the machine prints. The standard description holds how it works.

state-letters.text: How does Turing write the state q3 in letters?

dccc.why: C counts symbols. A counts states.

d3.why: The standard description uses only letters and the semicolon.

daaa.why: A state is D, then A as many times as its number: three times for q3.

aaa.why: Every state and every symbol starts with D.

description-number.text: How does a standard description become a description number?

digits.text: Each letter is replaced by a digit, such as A by 1 and D by 3
digits.why: The line of letters then reads as one long number.

count.why: Counting would give the same number to many machines.

sum.text: The numbers of the states are added up
sum.why: A sum would lose the rules. The description number keeps every letter.

universal-tape.text: What does the universal machine 𝒰 need at the start of its tape?

description.text: The standard description of another machine
description.why: 𝒰 reads it and does the work of that machine.

nothing.text: Nothing: it knows every machine already
nothing.why: 𝒰 has one fixed rule table. The other machine comes from the tape.

own-table.text: A new rule table for 𝒰 itself
own-table.why: 𝒰 never changes. Only the tape changes.

many-numbers.text: Can one machine have more than one description number?

exactly-one.text: No, each machine has exactly one
exactly-one.why: Another order of the rules gives another number for the same machine.

only-if-stops.why: Every machine has a description number, whether it stops or not.

yes.text: Yes, for example with its rules in another order
yes.why: Turing gives two numbers for his first machine. But each number describes only one machine.
